items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I played for a very short while with Roy Eldridge and his brother, Joe.

ctx.x: And then you say somewhere -- maybe in 1926 -- you ...

Yes. Well, actually, I played for a very short while with Roy Eldridge and his brother, Joe. They had an orchestra called the Elite Serenaders or Elite Syncopators, I don't know ... probably the Elite Serenaders.
And that was also in Pittsburgh?

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I hadn’t remembered before that I played in Fletcher’s band with Roy Eldridge

ctx.x: He eventually went to New York, himself. Is that true?
Yes, he eventually went to New York, and, gee, he played around New York for quite a bit. Unfortunately, I don’t know that he ever recorded. If so, no recording of his has

ever surfaced. But I know that people such as Roy Eldridge and some other people that were familiar with him at that time and had heard him, some of whom had played with him, spoke very wonderfully about him. But unfortunately, there’s nothing of his recording available.

items.title: 61530_Roy Eldridge oral history interview
items.q: And I think I was right, too -- although I didn't know I was right then. What they used to do, they'd... Well, they'd shake up the neighborhood, of course. It was a hell of a band. Eli Sarnees(?) (?) with the band once, and also Benny Carter.

ctx.x: Oh, that was before then! I told you, I got my first job playing Coleman Hawkins' chorus! Then after that, I was Benny Carter, you know -- him and Coleman. Then Buster Bailey.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Roy Eldridge Eldridge, who may be one of the few people around who would remember him

ctx.x: So I was just wondering -- I don't want to make a great deal out of just those few examples, but if there really was that much improvising, if improvising was ... I don't know quite how to put it ... as much a part of the jazzman's trade back then as it was now, what -- now, I think we assume that most people that we call 'jazzmen' are very, very capable improvisers. Was that the case then?

Yes, I think ... it's a pity that I don't ... well, I won't say that I don't, just -- that none of us have any examples of the playing of a trumpet player named Cuban Bennett, who was a first cousin of mine, and he was the first one that I think -- and Roy Eldridge Eldridge, who may be one
of the few people around who would remember him -- Roy Eldridge Ordige would attest to this -- he was probably the first musician that we heard that ran as we called it -- changes -- you know?
